subject: CHEEK and PERRY (1958)
object: CHEEK and PERRY (1958) reported a salt-wasting syndrome in infancy.

subject: DONNELL et al. (1959)
object: DONNELL et al. (1959) described pseudohypo-adrenalocorticism, a condition marked by renal sodium loss, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. They attributed it to insensitivity of the renal tubules to mineralocorticoids.

subject: RAINE and ROY (1962)
object: RAINE and ROY (1962) described a salt-losing syndrome in infancy, which they called pseudo-hypoadrenocorticalism.

subject: Armanini et al. (1985)
object: Armanini et al. (1985) studied 3 patients with pseudohypoaldosteronism. These were a 28-year-old index case from Melbourne and 2 siblings from Munich, aged 8 and 2 years, whose parents were first cousins. The younger sibling, a boy, was less severely affected than his sister. The authors described the syndrome as salt wasting and failure to thrive, usually presenting in infancy with high urinary sodium despite hyponatremia, together with hyperkalemia, hyperreninemia, and elevated aldosterone levels.

subject: Armanini et al. (1985)
object: Armanini et al. (1985) found that Percoll-separated monocytes from controls bound [3H]aldosterone with high affinity (Kd about 3 nM) and limited capacity (150 to 600 sites per cell). On repeated testing, no [3H]aldosterone binding was found in monocytes from patients 1 and 2. Patient 3, who was less severely affected, had 62 sites per cell, more than 2 SD below the control level. The parents of the Munich siblings had normal levels. The authors concluded that pseudohypoaldosteronism is caused by a Type I (mineralocorticoid) receptor defect that may be complete or partial.

subject: Armanini et al. (1985)
object: In the Munich family, the parents were first cousins and had normal monocyte aldosterone-receptor levels. Armanini et al. (1985) suggested that transmission of pseudohypoaldosteronism may be autosomal recessive.

subject: Hanukoglu (1991)
object: Hanukoglu (1991) described a kindred (kindred I) with type I pseudohypoaldosteronism in which the propositus presented in infancy with renal salt wasting, including vomiting, failure to thrive, short stature, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia, and responded dramatically to a high salt diet (2.5 g/day); sodium supplementation was discontinued at age 2 years. In 7 additional family members from 3 generations, clinical expression varied from asymptomatic to moderate.

subject: Hanukoglu (1991)
object: In affected members of kindred I (propositus, mother, and 2 brothers), Hanukoglu (1991) found that hyperaldosteronism persisted over 13 years while plasma renin activity decreased gradually to near-normal values, which was interpreted as development of tertiary hyperaldosteronism due to an autonomously functioning zona glomerulosa.

subject: Hanukoglu (1991)
object: Hanukoglu (1991) concluded that the pedigree of kindred I, with renal PHA I, was consistent with autosomal dominant transmission with variable expression.

subject: Hanukoglu (1991)
object: Hanukoglu (1991) described a second kindred in which the propositus, the offspring of a consanguineous marriage, developed severe renal salt losing at age 9 days with increased salivary and sweat electrolytes, indicating multiple target organ unresponsiveness to mineralocorticoids; life-threatening salt wasting recurred beyond age 2, and at 5 years she required 14 g/day salt. A sister died at 9 days with PHA symptoms, and the pedigree was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. From these kindreds and the literature, the author concluded that type I PHA comprises 2 clinically and genetically distinct entities with either renal or multiple target organ defects.

subject: Geller et al. (1998)
object: Geller et al. (1998) described pseudohypoaldosteronism type I (PHA1) as neonatal renal salt wasting with dehydration, hypotension, hyperkalemia and metabolic acidosis, even though aldosterone levels are high. They contrasted the severe autosomal recessive form, which persists into adulthood and is caused by ENaC loss-of-function mutations, with the autosomal dominant or sporadic form, which is milder and remits with age.

subject: Geller et al. (1998)
object: Geller et al. (1998) found no ENaC gene mutations in 6 dominant and 7 sporadic PHA1 kindreds, which pointed to mutations in other genes in the dominant form.

subject: Geller et al. (1998)
object: Geller et al. (1998) screened the mineralocorticoid receptor gene (MLR) in 13 dominant or sporadic PHA1 kindreds. They found heterozygous mutations in 1 sporadic and 4 dominant kindreds: 2 frameshift mutations (1 of them de novo), 2 premature termination codons and 1 splice donor mutation. The mutations segregated with PHA1 and were absent from unaffected subjects. The authors concluded that heterozygous MLR mutations cause PHA1.

subject: Tajima et al. (2000)
object: In affected members of a Japanese family with a renal form of PHA1, Tajima et al. (2000) identified by PCR and direct sequencing a heterozygous point mutation in the mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) gene changing codon 924 from leu (CTG) to pro (CCG) (L924P). In COS-1 cells transfected with a GRE-tk-CAT reporter, aldosterone increased CAT activity with wildtype receptor but had no effect with the L924P mutant. The authors suggested that mineralocorticoid resistance in this family was due to the missense mutation, the first missense MR mutation reported in renal PHA1.

subject: Tajima et al. (2000)
object: Tajima et al. (2000) noted that PHA1 is characterized by neonatal salt loss with dehydration, hypotension, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis despite elevated plasma aldosterone and PRA; the autosomal dominant form manifests milder salt wasting that gradually improves with age, in contrast to the severe multiorgan autosomal recessive form.

subject: Viemann et al. (2001)
object: In a patient with sporadic pseudohypoaldosteronism type I, Viemann et al. (2001) identified a frameshift mutation, Ins2871C, in exon 9 of the mineralocorticoid receptor gene (hMR). The mutation was not found in the patient's asymptomatic family members. It was the first mutation described in exon 9 and affects the last 27 amino acids of the hormone-binding domain.

subject: Viemann et al. (2001)
object: Viemann et al. (2001) found no mutation in the hMR gene in 5 affected patients from 2 families with autosomal dominant PHA I. They concluded that autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1 is genetically heterogeneous and involves other, as yet unidentified, genes.

subject: Sartorato et al. (2003)
object: Sartorato et al. (2003) analyzed the mineralocorticoid receptor (hMR) gene in 14 families with autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1, which is characterized by neonatal renal salt wasting and failure to thrive, and found 6 different heterozygous mutations. The authors concluded that hMR mutations are a common feature of autosomal dominant PHA1, since they were found in 70% of their familial cases.

subject: Sartorato et al. (2003)
object: In PHA1 families, Sartorato et al. (2003) found a heterozygous frameshift mutation in exon 2 of the hMR gene (insT1354). It is predicted to produce a truncated protein because of a premature stop codon.

subject: Sartorato et al. (2003)
object: In PHA1 families, Sartorato et al. (2003) found a heterozygous 8-bp deletion in exon 2 of the hMR gene (del8bp537). It causes a frameshift and is predicted to produce a truncated protein because of a premature stop codon.

subject: Sartorato et al. (2003)
object: In PHA1 families, Sartorato et al. (2003) found a heterozygous nonsense mutation in exon 4 of the hMR gene, C2157A, which changes cys645 to a stop codon (Cys645stop). It is predicted to produce a truncated protein.

subject: Sartorato et al. (2003)
object: In PHA1, Sartorato et al. (2003) found a heterozygous G633R missense mutation in the DNA-binding domain of hMR. The R633 mutant had reduced maximal transactivation, but its binding characteristics and ED50 of transactivation were comparable to wildtype hMR. The authors suggested that the mutation probably causes haploinsufficiency.

subject: Sartorato et al. (2003)
object: In PHA1, Sartorato et al. (2003) found a heterozygous Q776R missense mutation in the ligand-binding domain of hMR. The R776 mutant had reduced aldosterone binding and reduced ligand-dependent transactivation. The authors suggested that the mutation probably causes haploinsufficiency.

subject: Sartorato et al. (2003)
object: In PHA1, Sartorato et al. (2003) found a heterozygous L979P missense mutation in the ligand-binding domain of hMR. The P979 mutant did not bind aldosterone, had no ligand-dependent transactivation, and had a transdominant negative effect on wildtype hMR activity.

subject: Sartorato et al. (2003)
object: Sartorato et al. (2003) did not find hMR mutations in some families with PHA1. They noted that this points to the need for extensive investigation of the hMR gene and to other genes possibly involved in the disease.

subject: Riepe et al. (2006)
object: Riepe et al. (2006) identified 6 different heterozygous NR3C2 mutations in 6 patients with PHA1: a previously reported frameshift mutation (c.1131dupT), a second frameshift (c.2871dupC), 2 novel nonsense mutations generating a truncated receptor protein, and 2 missense mutations (S818L and E972G). The authors concluded that the data extended the spectrum of PHA1-causing NR3C2 mutations.

subject: Riepe et al. (2006)
object: Riepe et al. (2006) found that the NR3C2 frameshift mutation c.2871dupC, identified in heterozygous state in a PHA1 patient, showed no aldosterone binding and no transactivation because of a major change in receptor conformation.

subject: Riepe et al. (2006)
object: Riepe et al. (2006) showed that the heterozygous NR3C2 missense mutation S818L found in a PHA1 patient did not bind aldosterone, activate transcription, or translocate into the nucleus; 3-dimensional modeling showed a major displacement of several residues involved in aldosterone binding.

subject: Riepe et al. (2006)
object: Riepe et al. (2006) identified a novel heterozygous NR3C2 missense mutation, E972G, in a PHA1 patient; the mutant showed significantly lower ligand-binding affinity and only 9% of wildtype transcriptional activity, caused by major changes in receptor conformation.

subject: Pujo et al. (2007)
object: Pujo et al. (2007) carried out a comprehensive screen of the mineralocorticoid receptor gene (MR; NR3C2) in patients with PHA1. They searched coding regions, intron-exon junctions, and untranslated exons for nucleotide substitutions and also looked for large deletions. They found 22 MR gene abnormalities in 33 patients. The authors concluded that MR mutations are extremely frequent in PHA1 patients classified according to aldosterone and potassium levels.

subject: Pujo et al. (2007)
object: Pujo et al. (2007) suggested that a genocopy may exist in 3 PHA1 kindreds that had no MR mutation. They proposed that other patients without MR mutations might have different diseases that resemble PHA1 in the neonatal period.

subject: Pujo et al. (2007)
object: Pujo et al. (2007) described type 1 pseudohypoaldosteronism (PHA1) as a primary form of mineralocorticoid resistance. In the newborn it presents with salt wasting, hyperkalemia, and failure to thrive. Inactivating mutations in MR (NR3C2) cause the autosomal dominant form and some sporadic cases.
